confucius-09-15.translation: After I returned from Wei to Lu, the music was set right, and the ya and song each found their place.
confucius-09-15.note: One concrete accomplishment he claims for himself.

confucius-09-16.translation: Outside, to serve the high officers; at home, to serve father and elder brothers; in mourning, not to dare slacken; not to be undone by drink — what else is there in me?
confucius-09-16.note: Four ordinary things, and he says that is all there is.

confucius-09-17.translation: Standing by a stream he said: it passes like this, never stopping day or night.
confucius-09-17.note: Time said with nothing but running water.

confucius-09-18.translation: I have not met anyone who loves character the way they love beauty.
confucius-09-18.note: What pulls by itself against what has to be worked at.

confucius-09-19.translation: Like raising a mound: one basket short, and I stop — it is I who stopped. Like levelling ground: one basket tipped in, and I go on — it is I who went.
confucius-09-19.note: Not how far it got, but who it was that stopped.

confucius-09-20.translation: The one who never slackens when I speak to him — that is Hui.
confucius-09-20.note: Acting on what is heard is named as the rarest quality.

confucius-09-21.translation: Of Yan Yuan he said: what a loss. I saw him go forward; I never saw him stop.
confucius-09-21.note: Mourning a student, he records only that there was no stopping.

confucius-09-22.translation: Some sprout and never come into ear; some come into ear and never bear grain.
confucius-09-22.note: There is more than one place where it can stop.

confucius-09-23.translation: The young are to be held in awe — how do we know those to come will not match the present? But if by forty or fifty nothing has been heard of them, they are not to be held in awe either.
confucius-09-23.note: He rates youth highly and sets a deadline on it in the same breath.

confucius-09-24.translation: Can one not follow words of correction? What matters is changing. Can one not be pleased by gentle words? What matters is unpacking them. Pleased and never unpacking, following and never changing — with such a person I can do nothing.
confucius-09-24.note: He points at the gap between agreeing and changing.

confucius-09-25.translation: Put loyalty and reliability at the centre, do not take as friends those you cannot learn from, and when you are wrong do not shrink from changing.
confucius-09-25.note: A line from Book 1, recorded again here.

confucius-09-26.translation: An army of three divisions can be robbed of its general; one ordinary man cannot be robbed of his will.
confucius-09-26.note: The large and the small are turned around.

confucius-09-27.translation: In a worn padded coat, standing beside men in fox and badger furs and not ashamed — that would be You. Not harming, not coveting: how could that not be good? Zilu recited it all his life. The Master said: that way — is it enough to call good?
confucius-09-27.note: The praise gets memorised, so he raises the bar another notch.

confucius-09-28.translation: Only when the year turns cold do we know that pine and cypress are the last to wither.
confucius-09-28.note: What looked alike separates only when conditions worsen.

confucius-09-29.translation: The wise are not confused, the humane are not anxious, the brave are not afraid.
confucius-09-29.note: Each of the three virtues is defined by what it removes.

confucius-09-30.translation: You may study with someone and not go toward the way with them; go toward it and not stand with them; stand with them and not weigh things with them.
confucius-09-30.note: How far people can go together, cut into four stages. The last is the hardest.

confucius-09-31.translation: The flowers of the tangdi sway and turn. How should I not think of you? Your house is far. The Master said: he simply was not thinking of her. What distance is there?
confucius-09-31.note: A song that blames the distance is turned back into a question about wanting.

confucius-10-01.translation: In his home village Confucius was deferential, as if he could not speak. In the ancestral temple and at court he spoke readily, but with care.
confucius-10-01.note: The same man speaks differently by setting. It is not asked which is the real one.

confucius-10-02.translation: At court, speaking with the lower officers he was easy and frank; with the higher officers, upright. In the ruler's presence he was reverent, and yet composed.
confucius-10-02.note: Three different bearings, sorted by who was across from him.

confucius-10-03.translation: When the ruler had him receive guests, his face composed and his steps careful, he bowed to those beside him, hands turning left and right, his robe hanging straight before and behind. Hurrying forward, he was like a bird with spread wings. When the guests had gone he always reported back: the guests did not look round.
confucius-10-03.note: The task is closed by a report. That last sentence is the full stop on the procedure.

confucius-10-04a.translation: Entering the palace gate he bent as if there were no room for him. He did not stand in the middle of the gateway, nor tread on the threshold. Passing the ruler's place, his face composed, his steps careful, his words as if insufficient. Gathering his robe to climb to the hall he bent low, holding his breath as if not breathing.
confucius-10-04a.note: Movement by movement. Reverence is recorded only as what the body did.

confucius-10-04b.translation: Coming out and down one step, his face relaxed and brightened. At the bottom of the stairs he hurried forward like a bird with spread wings, and back at his place he was reverent again.
confucius-10-04b.note: Even the point where the tension lets go is written down.

confucius-10-05.translation: Holding the jade tablet he bent as if its weight were too much. Raising it as in a bow, lowering it as in handing over; his face tense, his feet in small steps as if following a line. At the presentation of gifts his face eased; in private audience he was cheerful.
confucius-10-05.note: The public face and the private one are set side by side at the end.

confucius-10-06a.translation: He did not trim with dark blue or maroon, nor make everyday clothes of red or purple. In heat he wore a single layer of fine or coarse linen, but always with an outer robe to go out. Black coat with lambskin, white with fawn, yellow with fox. The everyday fur coat was long, with the right sleeve short.
confucius-10-06a.note: A dress code. The right sleeve was shortened so the arm could work.

confucius-10-06b.translation: He always had a nightgown, one and a half times his height. At home he sat on thick fox and badger. Out of mourning, there was no ornament he did not wear. Unless it was a court skirt, he had it cut down. He did not pay condolences in lambskin and a black cap. On the first of the month he always went to court in court dress.
confucius-10-06b.note: The clause in parentheses sits in a different place in different editions.

confucius-10-07.translation: For fasting he always had a clean linen robe. Fasting, he changed what he ate and moved where he sat.
confucius-10-07.note: A change of mind is marked by clothes, food and place.

confucius-10-08a.translation: He did not object to finely milled rice, nor to thinly sliced meat. Rice gone sour, fish gone soft, meat gone off — he did not eat. Bad in colour, he did not eat; bad in smell, he did not eat. Badly cooked, he did not eat; out of season, he did not eat. Not cut straight, he did not eat; without the right sauce, he did not eat.
confucius-10-08a.note: A long list of refusals. Not a palate but a set of standards.

confucius-10-08b.translation: However much meat, he did not let it outweigh the rice. With wine alone he set no limit, but never to the point of disorder. He did not eat bought wine or market-dried meat. He did not clear the ginger away, but did not eat much of it. Meat from the state sacrifice did not stay overnight; sacrificial meat at home did not pass three days, and after three days he did not eat it.
confucius-10-08b.note: For wine alone no quantity is fixed; instead the limit is set by a condition.

confucius-10-08c.translation: He did not converse while eating, nor talk once in bed. Even with coarse rice, vegetable broth and melon, when he made the offering he was always reverent.
confucius-10-08c.note: However plain the table, the bearing is not scaled down.

confucius-10-09.translation: If the mat was not straight, he did not sit.
confucius-10-09.note: A record six characters long. The same standard reaches the smallest thing.

confucius-10-10.translation: At the village drinking, he left only after those with staffs had gone. At the village exorcism he stood on the eastern steps in court dress.
confucius-10-10.note: He keeps his place even at a rite he does not hold with.

confucius-10-11.translation: Sending greetings to someone in another state, he bowed twice as he saw the messenger off. When Kangzi sent medicine he bowed and accepted it, saying: I do not know this, so I dare not taste it.
confucius-10-11.note: He accepts it and does not take it, and does not hide that.

confucius-10-12.translation: The stables burned. Returning from court the Master said: was anyone hurt? He did not ask about the horses.
confucius-10-12.note: What he did not ask is recorded, so that what he asked first stands out.

confucius-10-13a.translation: When the ruler sent food, he straightened his mat and tasted it first. When the ruler sent raw meat, he cooked it and offered it to the ancestors. When the ruler sent a live animal, he kept it. Eating in attendance on the ruler, when the ruler made the offering he ate first. Ill, and visited by the ruler, he lay with his head to the east, his court robe over him and his sash laid across.
confucius-10-13a.note: Even sick in bed, he arranges himself for the rite.

confucius-10-13b.translation: Summoned by the ruler, he set off on foot without waiting for the carriage to be yoked.
confucius-10-13b.note: The response is shown by removing the wait.

confucius-10-14.translation: Entering the great temple, he asked about everything.
confucius-10-14.note: The line also stands in Book 3. Here only the fact is left, with no explanation.

confucius-10-15.translation: When a friend died with nowhere to go, he said: let the coffin rest here. Of a friend's gifts, even carriages and horses, he did not bow unless it was sacrificial meat.
confucius-10-15.note: He lightens the formality in receiving and gives up his own house in sending off.

confucius-10-16a.translation: He did not sleep like a corpse, nor stand on ceremony at home. Seeing someone in mourning, however familiar, he always changed his face. Seeing someone in ceremonial cap or someone blind, however private the setting, he always showed form. He bowed from the carriage to those in mourning, and to those carrying the census boards. When a full meal was set out, he always changed countenance and rose.
confucius-10-16a.note: The closer the relation, the more the form is kept.

confucius-10-16b.translation: At a sudden thunderclap or a fierce wind, he always changed countenance.
confucius-10-16b.note: Not only before people. Before the weather as well.

confucius-10-17.translation: Mounting the carriage he stood straight and took the strap. Inside he did not look back, did not speak fast, did not point.
confucius-10-17.note: Three things not done, and that is the record of how he rode.

confucius-10-18.translation: Startled, it rose, circled, and settled again. He said: the hen pheasant on the ridge — she knows her moment, she knows her moment. Zilu held one out to him; he sniffed three times and rose.
confucius-10-18.note: The last passage of Book 10 and the most disputed. Some take the text to be missing characters.

confucius-11-01.translation: Those who came to ritual and music first are called rustics; those who came later are called gentlemen. If I were to use them, I would follow the first.
confucius-11-01.note: Offered polish or roughness, he takes the rough.

confucius-11-02a.translation: Those who followed me in Chen and Cai are none of them at my door now. In conduct: Yan Yuan, Min Ziqian, Ran Boniu, Zhonggong. In speech: Zai Wo, Zigong. In government: Ran You, Jilu.
confucius-11-02a.note: A roster of students sorted by field.

confucius-11-02b.note: The last entry on the roster.

confucius-11-03.translation: Hui is no help to me. There is nothing I say that does not please him.
confucius-11-03.note: He misses being argued with. Praise and regret in one sentence.

confucius-11-04.translation: How filial Min Ziqian is. No one finds a gap in what his parents and brothers say of him.
confucius-11-04.note: The proof is not his conduct but that his family's account never wavers.

confucius-11-05.translation: Nan Rong repeated the Baigui ode three times over, and Confucius gave him his elder brother's daughter.
confucius-11-05.note: The Baigui says a flaw in speech cannot be ground away. He judged the man by the line he kept repeating.

confucius-11-06.translation: Ji Kangzi asked: which of your students loves learning? Confucius answered: there was Yan Hui, who loved learning. Sadly his life was short and he died. Now there is none.
confucius-11-06.note: Shorter than the same exchange in Book 6. A version with the explanation stripped out.

confucius-11-07a.translation: When Yan Yuan died, his father Yan Lu asked for the Master's carriage to make an outer coffin.
confucius-11-07a.note: The refusal that follows only makes sense with this request in front of it.

confucius-11-07b.translation: Gifted or not, each speaks of his own son. When my son Li died there was a coffin but no outer coffin. I did not go on foot to provide one, because I follow at the back of the officers and cannot go on foot.
confucius-11-07b.note: Not even for his dearest student does he overstep the form. He cites his own son first.

confucius-11-08.translation: When Yan Yuan died the Master said: alas, heaven is destroying me. Heaven is destroying me.
confucius-11-08.note: A student's death is spoken of as his own undoing.

confucius-11-09.translation: When Yan Yuan died the Master wailed with abandon. A follower said: you are overcome. He said: am I overcome? If not for this man, for whom?
confucius-11-09.note: The man who taught restraint is not restrained here.

confucius-11-10.translation: When Yan Yuan died the disciples wanted a lavish burial. The Master said: no. They buried him lavishly. The Master said: Hui looked on me as a father, and I could not look on him as a son. It was not I — it was you.
confucius-11-10.note: He takes responsibility for failing to stop it and still records who did it.

confucius-11-11.translation: Jilu asked about serving the spirits. The Master said: you cannot yet serve people; how could you serve spirits? He said: may I ask about death? Said: you do not yet know life; how would you know death?
confucius-11-11.note: He is not deferring the answer. He is putting the questions back in order.

confucius-11-12.translation: Min Ziqian in attendance was upright; Zilu was bold; Ran You and Zigong were easy and frank. The Master was glad. Someone like You will not die a natural death.
confucius-11-12.note: In the middle of his gladness he foresees one man's end. Zilu did die in a revolt.

confucius-11-13.translation: The men of Lu were rebuilding the Long Treasury. Min Ziqian said: why not keep to the old one? Why must it be rebuilt? The Master said: that man does not speak, but when he does he hits the mark.
confucius-11-13.note: One remark from a man who says little, written down on its own.

confucius-11-14.translation: The Master said: what is You's zither doing at my door? The disciples stopped respecting Zilu. The Master said: You has climbed to the hall. He has simply not entered the inner room.
confucius-11-14.note: When the rebuke starts turning into contempt, he corrects it at once.

confucius-11-15.translation: Zigong asked: which is better, Shi or Shang? The Master said: Shi goes too far, Shang falls short. Then is Shi the better? Going too far is the same as falling short.
confucius-11-15.note: He refuses the arithmetic in which further along means better.

confucius-11-16.translation: The Ji family was richer than the Duke of Zhou, and Qiu gathered taxes for them and added to it. The Master said: he is none of mine. Sound the drum and denounce him, my boys.
confucius-11-16.note: He cuts a student off in public. One of the harshest lines in the book.

confucius-11-17.translation: Chai is simple, Shen is slow, Shi is one-sided, You is rough.
confucius-11-17.note: Four students, one word of fault each.

confucius-11-18.translation: Hui came near it, and was often empty. Si would not accept his lot and made money; his guesses often hit.
confucius-11-18.note: Two students set side by side, with no verdict on which is better.

confucius-11-19.translation: Zizhang asked about the way of the good man. The Master said: he does not tread in others' tracks, and so he does not enter the inner room either.
confucius-11-19.note: Natural goodness on its own does not get you all the way in.

confucius-11-20.translation: If you side with someone because his talk is solid — is he a person of character, or just someone with a grave face?
confucius-11-20.note: The risk of judging on speech alone, put as a question.

confucius-11-21a.translation: Zilu asked: should one act on what one hears? The Master said: your father and elder brother are alive; how would you act straight off on what you hear? Ran You asked: should one act on what one hears? Act on it.
confucius-11-21a.note: The same question, opposite answers. The reason comes in the next passage.

confucius-11-21b.translation: Gongxi Hua said: You asked whether to act on what he hears and you said his father and brother are alive; Qiu asked the same and you said act on it. I am puzzled, and dare to ask.
confucius-11-21b.note: A student sees the contradiction and asks on the spot.

confucius-11-21c.translation: Qiu holds back, so I pushed him forward; You takes on two men's share, so I pulled him back.
confucius-11-21c.note: One principle applied in opposite directions. Teaching shown as prescription.

confucius-11-22.translation: In danger at Kuang, Yan Yuan fell behind. The Master said: I thought you were dead. He said: while you live, how would I dare to die?
confucius-11-22.note: Two short lines hold the whole relation.

confucius-11-23a.translation: Ji Ziran asked: can Zhong You and Ran Qiu be called great ministers? The Master said: I thought you would ask about something unusual, and you ask about You and Qiu. A great minister serves his ruler by the way, and stops when he cannot.
confucius-11-23a.note: He sets the definition first, then holds the two men up against it.

confucius-11-23b.translation: As things are, You and Qiu may be called ministers who fill a place. Then would they just follow orders? In killing a father or a ruler, they would not follow.
confucius-11-23b.note: He rates them low and still says they would hold the last line.

confucius-11-24.translation: Zilu made Zigao steward of Bi. The Master said: you are ruining another man's son. Zilu said: there are people there, there are altars of state — must one read books before it counts as learning? The Master said: this is why I dislike a glib tongue.
confucius-11-24.note: He does not answer the plausible retort. He points at the glibness of it.

confucius-11-25a.translation: Zilu, Zengxi, Ran You and Gongxi Hua were sitting with him. The Master said: do not hold back because I am a day older than you. You say you are not recognised. If someone did recognise you, what would you do?
confucius-11-25a.note: The opening of the longest scene in the book. He clears the formality away first.

confucius-11-25b.translation: Zilu answered straight off: a state of a thousand chariots squeezed between great powers, hit by armies and then by famine — let me manage it, and in three years the people would have courage and know which way to go. The Master smiled.
confucius-11-25b.note: The smile says more than the answer does.

confucius-11-25c.translation: Qiu, what about you? A district of sixty or seventy li, or fifty or sixty — let me manage it, and in three years the people would have enough. As for ritual and music, I would wait for a person of character. Chi, what about you?
confucius-11-25c.note: Each answer steps the scale and the claim down a notch.

confucius-11-25d.translation: He said: not that I can do it — I would like to learn. At services in the ancestral temple, or at a gathering of the lords, in robe and cap, I would like to be a minor assistant. Dian, what about you? The zither had grown sparse; with a last ringing note he set it down and rose.
confucius-11-25d.note: The scene turns not on an answer but on a zither being put down.

confucius-11-25e.translation: He said: it is different from what the three of them set out. The Master said: what harm? Each is just saying what he is after. He said: in late spring, when the spring clothes are finished, with five or six grown men and six or seven boys,
confucius-11-25e.note: In a conversation about affairs of state, someone starts talking about a season.

confucius-11-25f.translation: to bathe in the Yi, catch the breeze at the rain altar, and come home singing. The Master sighed and said: I am with Dian.
confucius-11-25f.note: After answers about taking charge of states, he picks the one that takes charge of nothing.

confucius-12-01a.translation: Yan Yuan asked about humaneness. Master yourself and return to ritual — that is humaneness. Do it for a single day and the world turns to humaneness. Humaneness comes from oneself; does it come from others? Yan Yuan said: may I ask for the particulars.
confucius-12-01a.note: He hears the principle and immediately asks for the items.

confucius-12-01b.translation: Do not look at what is not ritual, do not listen to what is not ritual, do not speak what is not ritual, do not move by what is not ritual. Yan Yuan said: slow as I am, I will work at these words.
confucius-12-01b.note: The principle is broken into four senses and so becomes doable today.

confucius-12-02a.note: The same question gets a different answer, because the asker is different.

confucius-12-02b.translation: Outside your gate, behave as if meeting an honoured guest; employ the people as if conducting a great sacrifice. What you do not want, do not do to others. Then there is no resentment in the state and none at home. Zhonggong said: slow as I am, I will work at these words.
confucius-12-02b.note: Here humaneness is cast as a posture toward others, paired with the answer given to Yan Yuan.

confucius-12-03.translation: Sima Niu asked about humaneness. The Master said: the humane are slow of speech. Is being slow of speech enough to be called humane? The Master said: when the doing is hard, how could the saying not be slow?
confucius-12-03.note: A third man, a third answer. A prescription fitted to someone who talks a lot.

confucius-12-04.translation: Sima Niu asked about the person of character. They are without anxiety and without fear. Is being without anxiety and fear enough? Looking inward he finds nothing wrong — what is there to be anxious about, what to fear?
confucius-12-04.note: The same push-back, answered the same way: he gives the cause, not the result.

confucius-12-05a.translation: Sima Niu said in distress: everyone has brothers; only I have none.
confucius-12-05a.note: The man just told not to be anxious brings out his anxiety.

confucius-12-05b.translation: Zixia said: I have heard that life and death are allotted, and wealth and rank rest with heaven. If a person of character is reverent and makes no lapse, and is respectful and correct with others, then within the four seas all are brothers. Why should he worry about having none?
confucius-12-05b.note: Not the teacher but a fellow student answers. Instead of filling the lack, he widens the circle.

confucius-12-06.translation: Zizhang asked about clear sight. Slanders that soak in and complaints that touch the skin — if these do not get through, that may be called clear sight. Slanders that soak in and complaints that touch the skin — if these do not get through, that may be called far sight.
confucius-12-06.note: The same condition stated twice with only the conclusion changed. Seeing clearly and seeing far are one thing.

confucius-12-07a.translation: Zigong asked about government. Enough food, enough arms, and the people's trust. Zigong said: if one had to be given up, which first? Give up the arms.
confucius-12-07a.note: Asked to rank them, he lets go first of the one that looks strongest.

confucius-12-07b.translation: And if one more had to go? Give up the food. From of old all have died; but without the people's trust there is no standing.
confucius-12-07b.note: Trust is kept behind even food. A way of deciding what is held to the end.

confucius-12-08a.translation: Ji Zicheng said: a person of character is substance and nothing more; what use is polish? Zigong said: a pity — what you say sounds like a person of character, but four horses cannot catch the tongue. Polish is as substance, substance is as polish.
confucius-12-08a.note: He begins by noting that a word once out cannot be caught.

confucius-12-08b.translation: A tiger's or leopard's hide, stripped of hair, is the same as a dog's or sheep's.
confucius-12-08b.note: Take the markings off and the distinction goes. The image carries the point.

confucius-12-09a.translation: Duke Ai asked You Ruo: the harvest is bad and we are short; what should be done? You Ruo answered: why not the tenth? He said: with two tenths I am still short; how could I take a tenth?
confucius-12-09a.note: Where the drift is toward raising the tax, he answers by lowering it.

confucius-12-09b.translation: He answered: if the people have enough, with whom would the ruler not have enough? If the people do not, with whom would the ruler have enough?
confucius-12-09b.note: He ties the ruler's accounts to the people's and makes them one.

confucius-12-10a.translation: Zizhang asked how to raise character and tell confusion apart. Put loyalty and reliability at the centre and move toward what is right: that raises character. Loving someone you want them to live, hating them you want them dead; to have wanted them to live and then to want them dead — that is confusion.
confucius-12-10a.note: Confusion is defined as wanting opposite things for the same person.

confucius-12-10b.translation: Truly not for riches, only because it is different.
confucius-12-10b.note: Two lines lifted from the Odes. They do not connect to what is around them and are generally taken as misplaced.

confucius-12-11a.translation: Duke Jing of Qi asked Confucius about government.
confucius-12-11a.note: The question that leads to one of the shortest answers.

confucius-12-11b.translation: Confucius answered: let the ruler be a ruler, the minister a minister, the father a father, the son a son. The duke said: well said. If truly the ruler is no ruler, the minister no minister, the father no father, the son no son, then though there were grain, would I get to eat it?
confucius-12-11b.note: Eight characters as the answer, and the listener unfolds it himself.

confucius-12-12.translation: The one who could settle a case on a word or two would be You. Zilu never let a promise sit overnight.
confucius-12-12.note: After the praise, one line giving the habit behind it.

confucius-12-13.translation: In hearing lawsuits I am like anyone else. What I would want is that there be no lawsuits.
confucius-12-13.note: The goal is not handling them well but their not arising.

confucius-12-14.translation: Zizhang asked about government. Hold the post without slackening, and carry it out with loyalty.
confucius-12-14.note: Not an institution but two states of the person holding the post.

confucius-12-15.translation: Learn widely in the texts and rein it in with ritual. Then one will not go astray.
confucius-12-15.note: A line from Book 6, recorded again here.

confucius-12-16.translation: A person of character brings out what is good in others and does not bring out what is bad. A lesser one does the reverse.
confucius-12-16.note: People are sorted by which direction they work on others.

confucius-12-17.translation: Ji Kangzi asked Confucius about government. He answered: to govern is to set right. If you lead with rightness, who would dare not be right?
confucius-12-17.note: The answer starts from the word itself: governing and setting right share a root.

confucius-12-18.translation: Ji Kangzi was troubled by thieves and asked Confucius. He answered: if you yourself did not covet, they would not steal even if you paid them to.
confucius-12-18.note: Asked about policing, he turns it back on the asker's own appetite.

confucius-12-19a.translation: Ji Kangzi asked: what if I killed those without the way to bring on those who have it? Confucius answered: you are governing — what need is there to kill? Want good yourself and the people will be good. The character of those above is wind;
confucius-12-19a.note: A question that reaches for killing is turned by an image of wind and grass.

confucius-12-19b.translation: the character of those below is grass. When the wind passes over the grass, it bends.
confucius-12-19b.note: That those below follow those above, made into a single picture.

confucius-12-20a.translation: Zizhang asked: how must a scholar be to be called accomplished? The Master said: what do you mean by accomplished? Zizhang said: known throughout the state, known throughout the clan.
confucius-12-20a.note: Before answering, he asks what the word is supposed to mean.

confucius-12-20b.translation: That is being known, not being accomplished. The accomplished are straight in substance and love what is right, weigh what is said and read the face, and think to put themselves below others. Such a one is accomplished in the state and in the clan.
confucius-12-20b.note: Being known and actually getting through are set apart.

confucius-12-20c.translation: The one who is known takes on humaneness in appearance while his conduct departs from it, and settles into it without a doubt. Such a one is known in the state and in the clan.
confucius-12-20c.note: The sharpest words are without a doubt.

confucius-12-21a.translation: Fan Chi, walking with him below the rain altar, said: may I ask about raising character, correcting what is hidden and bad, and telling confusion apart? The Master said: a good question. To put the work first and the gain after — is that not raising character?
confucius-12-21a.note: Three things asked at once, answered one at a time as counter-questions.

confucius-12-21b.translation: To attack your own faults and not others' — is that not correcting what is hidden? In a single morning's anger to forget yourself, and your parents along with you — is that not confusion?
confucius-12-21b.note: Confusion is explained not in the abstract but as the path anger travels.

confucius-12-22a.translation: Fan Chi asked about humaneness. Love people. About wisdom. Know people. Fan Chi did not follow, and the Master said: raise the straight and set them above the crooked, and the crooked can be made straight.
confucius-12-22a.note: Two-word answers; when they do not land, he restates them as something to do.

confucius-12-22b.translation: Fan Chi withdrew and saw Zixia: just now I asked the Master about wisdom and he said, raise the straight and set them above the crooked, and the crooked can be made straight. What does it mean? Zixia said: how rich those words are.
confucius-12-22b.note: The one who did not follow goes and asks a fellow student.

confucius-12-22c.translation: When Shun held the realm he chose from among the many and raised Gao Yao, and the inhumane withdrew. When Tang held the realm he chose from among the many and raised Yi Yin, and the inhumane withdrew.
confucius-12-22c.note: The same sentence twice over, proving the point by cases.

confucius-12-23.translation: Zigong asked about friends. Tell them in good faith and guide them well; when it will not do, stop, and do not bring disgrace on yourself.
confucius-12-23.note: Advice comes with a point at which to stop giving it.

confucius-12-24.translation: A person of character gathers friends through the texts, and through friends supports humaneness.
confucius-12-24.note: Learning, friendship and humaneness strung on one line.

confucius-13-01.translation: Zilu asked about government. Go before them, and work at it. He asked for more: do not slacken.
confucius-13-01.note: Asked for more, he adds not another item but keeping at it.

confucius-13-02.translation: Zhonggong, steward to the Ji family, asked about government. Put the officers first, pardon small faults, raise the worthy and able. He said: how do I know the worthy and able to raise them? Raise those you know. Those you do not — will others leave them aside?
confucius-13-02.note: He lifts the burden of having to know everyone before acting.

confucius-13-03a.translation: Zilu said: if the ruler of Wei were waiting for you to govern, what would you do first? The Master said: set names right. Zilu said: is that so? How roundabout you are. What is there to set right? The Master said: how crude you are, You.
confucius-13-03a.note: The most practical question gets the most abstract answer, and the student says so to his face.

confucius-13-03b.translation: A person of character leaves a blank where he does not know. If names are not right, speech does not follow; if speech does not follow, work is not done; if work is not done, ritual and music do not flourish; if they do not flourish, punishments miss the mark.
confucius-13-03b.note: He links it as a chain, from names all the way to punishments.

confucius-13-03c.translation: If punishments miss the mark, the people have nowhere to put hand or foot. So what a person of character names, he must be able to say; what he says, he must be able to do. In his speech there is simply nothing slipshod.
confucius-13-03c.note: The answer that looked abstract comes down to words matching deeds.

confucius-13-04a.translation: Fan Chi asked to learn farming. The Master said: I am no match for an old farmer. He asked to learn gardening: I am no match for an old gardener. When Fan Chi had gone the Master said: what a small man Fan Xu is. If those above love ritual, the people dare not be disrespectful;
confucius-13-04a.note: He does not block the learning; he says that is not where this man's place is.

confucius-13-04b.translation: If those above love what is right, the people dare not disobey; if they love reliability, the people dare not withhold their hearts. Then people from the four quarters will come with their children on their backs. What need of farming?
confucius-13-04b.note: The work of that post is not to plant but to make people come.

confucius-13-05.translation: Recite the three hundred Odes, and then be given government and not get through, or be sent abroad and not manage the exchanges alone — however many you know, what are they for?
confucius-13-05.note: What has been memorised is tested against what it does.

confucius-13-06.translation: If he himself is upright, things get done without orders; if he is not, they are not followed though he orders.
confucius-13-06.note: The force of an order is located outside the order.

confucius-13-07.translation: The governments of Lu and Wei are brothers.
confucius-13-07.note: Their situations resemble each other, and not only in a good sense.

confucius-13-08.translation: Of Prince Jing of Wei he said: he managed his household well. When he first had something: this will do. When he had a little: this is about complete. When he was well off: this is fine enough.
confucius-13-08.note: The same phrasing three times. As the holdings grow, the bar does not.

confucius-13-09.translation: Going to Wei with Ran You driving, the Master said: how many they are. Ran You said: and once they are many, what next? Make them well off. And once they are well off? Teach them.
confucius-13-09.note: The order is made explicit. Teaching comes after the living is made.

confucius-13-10.translation: If someone would truly employ me, in a year it would do; in three years there would be something achieved.
confucius-13-10.note: A man who is not employed names a timetable.

confucius-13-11.translation: Let good men govern a state for a hundred years and cruelty could be overcome and killing done away with. How true that saying is.
confucius-13-11.note: Change is given a scale, and the scale is a century.

confucius-13-12.translation: Even with a true king, it would take a generation before humaneness.
confucius-13-12.note: Even under the best conditions, he allows for time.

confucius-13-13.translation: If he sets himself right, what difficulty is there in government? If he cannot set himself right, how will he set others right?
confucius-13-13.note: The same thought as before, recast as two questions.

confucius-13-14.translation: Ran You came back late from court. The Master asked: why so late? He said: there was government business. The Master said: that was family business. Had it been government, I would have heard of it, even unemployed as I am.
confucius-13-14.note: He corrects the use of a word, catching a family's affairs being called government.

confucius-13-15a.translation: Duke Ding asked: is there one word that could raise a state? Confucius answered: words do not come that close. But people say, it is hard to be a ruler and not easy to be a minister.
confucius-13-15a.note: He first denies that one word can do it, then offers one.

confucius-13-15b.translation: If he knows how hard it is to be a ruler, is that not close to one word raising a state? He said: is there one word that could lose a state? Confucius answered: words do not come that close.
confucius-13-15b.note: The other side asked in the same form.

confucius-13-15c.translation: People say: there is no pleasure in being a ruler, except that no one crosses what he says. If what he says is good and no one crosses it, is that not good? If it is not good and no one crosses it, is that not close to one word losing a state?
confucius-13-15c.note: The danger named is the state of having no one contradict you.

confucius-13-16.translation: The Duke of She asked about government. Those near are pleased, and those far away come.
confucius-13-16.note: The result is measured not in figures but in which way people move.

confucius-13-17.translation: Zixia, steward of Jufu, asked about government. Do not want speed, and do not look at small gains. Want speed and you do not arrive; look at small gains and the large work is not done.
confucius-13-17.note: Two prohibitions, each with its reason attached right away.

confucius-13-18.translation: The Duke of She said: in my district there is a man of upright conduct — his father stole a sheep and the son testified against him. Confucius said: in my district the upright are different. The father covers for the son and the son for the father, and uprightness lies in that.
confucius-13-18.note: Two definitions of uprightness meet head-on: the law on one side, the family on the other.

confucius-13-19.translation: Fan Chi asked about humaneness. At home be respectful, in work be reverent, with others be loyal. Even among the border peoples these cannot be dropped.
confucius-13-19.note: Humaneness converted into three postures that do not depend on where you are.

confucius-13-20a.translation: Zigong asked: how must one be to be called a scholar? The Master said: to feel shame in his own conduct, and sent abroad not to disgrace his ruler's commission — that may be called a scholar. He said: may I ask the next.
confucius-13-20a.note: He answers from the top grade and works downward.

confucius-13-20b.translation: That his clan calls him filial and his village calls him deferential. May I ask the next. Whose word is always kept and whose action always carried through — stubbornly so, a small man; still, he may be put next.
confucius-13-20b.note: Keeping your word is placed lowest. The inflexibility is counted as the flaw.

confucius-13-20c.translation: And what of those in government now? Ah — men of a peck and a basket. What is there to count?
confucius-13-20c.note: They do not even make the third grade.

confucius-13-21.translation: If I cannot find those who walk the middle to go with, then surely the ardent or the restrained: the ardent press forward and take, the restrained have things they will not do.
confucius-13-21.note: Even among those who lean one way, he finds what each is good for.

confucius-13-22.translation: The southerners say: a person without constancy cannot even be a shaman or a healer. Well said. And: not constant in character, he will meet with disgrace. The Master said: he simply does not consult the oracle.
confucius-13-22.note: The last line is read in different ways; most take it as meaning the case is clear without divining.

confucius-13-23.translation: A person of character is in harmony without becoming the same; a lesser one becomes the same without being in harmony.
confucius-13-23.note: Real agreement keeps differences; false agreement erases them and joins no one.

confucius-13-24a.translation: Zigong asked: if everyone in the village likes him, how is that? Not yet. If everyone in the village dislikes him? Not yet.
confucius-13-24a.note: He distrusts unanimity in either direction.

confucius-13-24b.translation: Better that the good of the village like him and the bad dislike him.
confucius-13-24b.note: The test offered is who it is that likes you.

confucius-13-25a.translation: A person of character is easy to serve and hard to please: please him off the way and he is not pleased; and in employing people he uses them to their capacity. A lesser one is hard to serve and easy to please: please him off the way and he is pleased;
confucius-13-25a.note: Easy to serve against easy to please, crossed over to separate the two.

confucius-13-25b.translation: and in employing people he demands everything of them.
confucius-13-25b.note: Set directly against using people to their capacity above.

confucius-13-26.translation: A person of character is at ease without being proud; a lesser one is proud without being at ease.
confucius-13-26.note: Two states that look alike are pulled apart.

confucius-13-27.translation: Firm, resolute, plain and slow of speech — these are near to humaneness.
confucius-13-27.note: Everything he names as near to humaneness is a quality that does not stand out.

confucius-13-28.translation: Zilu asked: how must one be to be called a scholar? Earnest and urging, and harmonious — that may be called a scholar. With friends, earnest and urging; with brothers, harmonious.
confucius-13-28.note: The same question Zigong asked, answered differently. This one is fitted to Zilu.

confucius-13-29.translation: Let good men teach the people for seven years, and they may be sent to arms.
confucius-13-29.note: Before sending them to fight, he fixes the length of the teaching first.

confucius-13-30.translation: To take people who have not been taught into battle is called throwing them away.
confucius-13-30.note: The reverse of the line before: sending them out unprepared is named abandonment.

confucius-14-01.translation: Xian asked about shame. The Master said: to take a salary when the state has the way; to take a salary when it does not — that is shame.
confucius-14-01.note: The same act becomes shameful depending on the circumstances.

confucius-14-02.translation: If one does not act on rivalry, boasting, resentment or craving, may that be called humane? The Master said: it may be called difficult. Whether it is humane, I do not know.
confucius-14-02.note: Refraining alone does not get you to humaneness.

confucius-14-03.translation: A scholar whose mind is on comfortable living falls short of being a scholar.
confucius-14-03.note: Qualification is decided by what is always on the mind.

confucius-14-04.translation: When the state has the way, speak boldly and act boldly. When it does not, act boldly and speak with reserve.
confucius-14-04.note: The conduct does not change; only the speech is adjusted.

confucius-14-05.translation: One with character is sure to have something to say; one with something to say is not sure to have character. The humane are sure to have courage; the courageous are not sure to be humane.
confucius-14-05.note: A relation that holds in one direction only, shown twice.

confucius-14-06a.translation: Nangong Kuo asked Confucius: Yi was a fine archer and Ao could haul a boat, and neither died a natural death. Yu and Ji farmed with their own hands and gained the realm. The Master did not answer.
confucius-14-06a.note: The silence is what gets recorded. The reason comes in the next passage.

confucius-14-06b.translation: When Nangong Kuo had gone the Master said: what a person of character he is. How he values character.
confucius-14-06b.note: The silence before was not disagreement.

confucius-14-07.translation: There may be a person of character who is not humane; there has never been a lesser one who is.
confucius-14-07.note: Holding the name does not guarantee the thing.

confucius-14-08.translation: If you love someone, can you spare them effort? If you are loyal to them, can you spare them instruction?
confucius-14-08.note: Caring for someone is kept apart from making things easy for them.

confucius-14-09.translation: In drafting a dispatch, Bi Chen made the first draft, Shishu went over it, the envoy Ziyu trimmed it, and Zichan of Dongli gave it polish.
confucius-14-09.note: One document through four hands. The credit is written out shared.

confucius-14-10.translation: Someone asked about Zichan: a generous man. About Zixi: that one, that one. About Guan Zhong: the man stripped the Bo family of three hundred households at Pian, and Bo ate coarse rice to the end of his days without a word of resentment.
confucius-14-10.note: The praise is delivered through the reaction of the man who was stripped.

confucius-14-11.translation: Poor and without resentment is hard; rich and without arrogance is easy.
confucius-14-11.note: He states plainly which of the two is the harder.

confucius-14-12.translation: Meng Gongchuo would do very well as an elder in the Zhao or Wei houses, but could not be a minister of Teng or Xue.
confucius-14-12.note: Not the size of the man but the fit between man and post.

confucius-14-13a.translation: Zilu asked about the complete person. With Zang Wuzhong's wisdom, Gongchuo's freedom from craving, Bian Zhuangzi's courage and Ran Qiu's accomplishment, finished off with ritual and music — that could be called a complete person.
confucius-14-13a.note: He first sets a bar so high it takes four men's strengths to clear.

confucius-14-13b.translation: And he said: why must it be so for a complete person today? Seeing gain, to think of what is right; seeing danger, to give one's life; and over a long-standing promise, not to forget what one always said — that too may be called a complete person.
confucius-14-13b.note: He lowers his own bar to a place where it can actually be met.

confucius-14-14a.translation: The Master asked Gongming Jia about Gongshu Wenzi: is it true he does not speak, does not laugh, does not take? Gongming Jia answered: whoever told you overstated it. He speaks when the time is right, and people do not tire of his speech;
confucius-14-14a.note: It was not abstaining but choosing the moment.

confucius-14-14b.translation: he laughs when there is joy, and people do not tire of his laughter; he takes when it is right, and people do not tire of his taking. The Master said: so it is. But is it really so?
confucius-14-14b.note: He accepts it, and still leaves one doubt standing.

confucius-14-15.translation: Zang Wuzhong used his hold on Fang to ask Lu to establish his heir. Though it is said he did not coerce his ruler, I do not believe it.
confucius-14-15.note: Whatever it is called, if the setup is pressure then it is pressure.

confucius-14-16.translation: Duke Wen of Jin was devious and not upright; Duke Huan of Qi was upright and not devious.
confucius-14-16.note: Two hegemons of the same rank, split by a single test.

confucius-14-17a.translation: Zilu said: when Duke Huan killed Prince Jiu, Shao Hu died with him and Guan Zhong did not. Was that not unhumane? The Master said: that Duke Huan assembled the lords nine times without war chariots was Guan Zhong's doing. Such was his humaneness.
confucius-14-17a.note: Dying for loyalty is weighed against what living made possible.

confucius-14-17b.note: The same words again, setting the verdict.

confucius-14-18a.translation: Zigong said: surely Guan Zhong was not humane? When Duke Huan killed Prince Jiu he could not die with him, and went on to serve the killer. The Master said: Guan Zhong served Duke Huan, made him leader of the lords and set the realm right at a stroke, and the people benefit from it to this day.
confucius-14-18a.note: Two students bring the same objection and get the same answer.

confucius-14-18b.translation: Without Guan Zhong we would wear our hair loose and fold our robes to the left. Is that like ordinary men and women keeping some small faith, hanging themselves in a ditch where no one knows of it?
confucius-14-18b.note: A small fidelity set directly against a large result.

confucius-14-19.translation: Zhuan, an officer who had been Gongshu Wenzi's retainer, rose to the court alongside him. Hearing of it the Master said: he may well be called Wen.
confucius-14-19.note: Raising a subordinate to his own level is taken as the ground for the title.

confucius-14-20.translation: The Master said Duke Ling of Wei was without the way. Kangzi said: then how has he not fallen? Confucius said: Zhongshu Yu handles the guests, Zhu Tuo the ancestral temple, Wangsun Jia the army. With that, how would he fall?
confucius-14-20.note: With no one at the top, a state still holds if each post is filled.

confucius-14-21.translation: One who says it without embarrassment will find the doing hard.
confucius-14-21.note: Words that come out easily are read as a warning sign.

confucius-14-22a.translation: Chen Chengzi killed Duke Jian. Confucius bathed and went to court and reported to Duke Ai: Chen Heng has killed his ruler; I ask that he be punished. The duke said: tell the three.
confucius-14-22a.note: That he bathed first is the line that carries the weight.

confucius-14-22b.translation: Confucius said: following at the back of the officers, I did not dare not report it. The ruler says, tell the three. He went to the three and told them; they said no. Confucius said: following at the back of the officers, I did not dare not report it.
confucius-14-22b.note: He says it twice. The measure is not the outcome but whether the duty was done.

confucius-14-23.translation: Zilu asked about serving a ruler. Do not deceive him, and stand up to him.
confucius-14-23.note: The condition of service is not obedience but not deceiving.

confucius-14-24.translation: A person of character gets through upward; a lesser one gets through downward.
confucius-14-24.note: The same effort, pointed in different directions.

confucius-14-25.translation: Those who learned in the old days did it for themselves; those who learn now do it for others.
confucius-14-25.note: Whether learning is aimed inward or outward.

confucius-14-26.translation: Qu Boyu sent a man to Confucius. Confucius sat with him and asked: what is your master doing? He answered: my master wishes to reduce his faults and has not managed it. When the man had gone the Master said: what a messenger. What a messenger.
confucius-14-26.note: An answer that lowers the master is what raises him.

confucius-14-27.translation: If you are not in the post, do not plan its business.
confucius-14-27.note: The line from Book 8, recorded here again unchanged.

confucius-14-28.translation: A person of character does not let his thoughts stray outside his position.
confucius-14-28.note: Zengzi picking up the line before and setting it down again.

confucius-14-29.translation: A person of character is ashamed when his words outrun his conduct.
confucius-14-29.note: The order of words and deeds comes up again and again in this book.

confucius-14-30.translation: There are three ways of the person of character, and I can do none of them: the humane are not anxious, the wise are not confused, the brave are not afraid. Zigong said: the Master is describing himself.
confucius-14-30.note: A disclaimer that a student reads as a self-portrait.

confucius-14-31.translation: Zigong was comparing people. The Master said: so Si is clever, is he? I have no time for it.
confucius-14-31.note: No direct rebuke. He states his own case and lets it reflect.

confucius-14-32.translation: Do not worry that others do not know you; worry that you are not able.
confucius-14-32.note: The same opening as in Book 1, with a different ending. The worry moves further inward.

confucius-14-33.translation: Not to anticipate deceit, not to guess at untrustworthiness, and yet to see it first — that is the worthy one.
confucius-14-33.note: It asks for not suspecting and for noticing, at the same time.

confucius-14-34.translation: Weisheng Mu said to Confucius: Qiu, why do you keep flitting about? Is it not a gift for talk? Confucius said: I do not presume to a gift for talk. I dislike rigidity.
confucius-14-34.note: He explains the wandering not by his own stubbornness but by a distaste for it.

confucius-14-35.translation: A fine horse is praised not for its strength but for its qualities.
confucius-14-35.note: Said of a horse, meant as a measure for people.

confucius-14-36.translation: Someone said: what about repaying resentment with kindness? The Master said: then with what would you repay kindness? Repay resentment with uprightness, and kindness with kindness.
confucius-14-36.note: Most editions read uprightness here; this one repeats kindness. The logic of the retort favours uprightness.

confucius-14-37.translation: No one knows me. Zigong said: how is it that no one knows you? The Master said: I do not resent heaven, I do not blame others; I learn from below and get through upward. What knows me is heaven.
confucius-14-37.note: Being unrecognised is not converted into resentment but left as it is.

confucius-14-38a.translation: Gongbo Liao slandered Zilu to Jisun. Zifu Jingbo reported it, saying: my lord has indeed been swayed by Gongbo Liao, but I have power enough to have his body exposed in the marketplace. The Master said: that the way will be carried out is fate;
confucius-14-38a.note: Offered revenge, he answers with the word fate.

confucius-14-38b.translation: that the way will be set aside is fate. What can Gongbo Liao do about fate?
confucius-14-38b.note: One man's interference is placed inside a larger frame and so disarmed.

confucius-14-39.translation: The worthy avoid the age; next, they avoid a place; next, a look; next, a word.

confucius-14-40.note: A single line following the one before, and it does not say who.

confucius-14-41.translation: Zilu spent the night at Shimen. The gatekeeper asked: where from? From the Kong house. He said: the one who knows it cannot be done and does it anyway?
confucius-14-41.note: A gatekeeper's line survives as the shortest summary of Confucius there is.

confucius-14-42a.translation: The Master was striking the stone chimes in Wei. A man passing the Kong gate with a basket said: there is a heart in that chiming. Then he said: how stiff — that clanking. If no one knows you, let it be, and have done.
confucius-14-42a.note: From the sound alone, he reads the man's situation.

confucius-14-42b.translation: Deep, wade in clothes; shallow, lift the hem. The Master said: how decisive. There would be no difficulty in that.
confucius-14-42b.note: Advice to adjust to the world, turned aside in a single line.

confucius-14-43.translation: Zizhang said: the Documents say Gaozong kept silence in mourning for three years. What does that mean? The Master said: why only Gaozong — the ancients all did so. When a ruler died, all the officers gathered their duties and took direction from the chief minister for three years.
confucius-14-43.note: An odd anecdote explained as the standing institution of the time.

confucius-14-44.translation: If those above love ritual, the people are easy to employ.
confucius-14-44.note: The way to get compliance is located in the bearing of those above.

confucius-14-45a.translation: Zilu asked about the person of character. Cultivate yourself in reverence. Is that all? Cultivate yourself so others are at ease. Is that all? Cultivate yourself so the people are at ease.
confucius-14-45a.note: All three begin from cultivating yourself. Only the reach widens.

confucius-14-45b.translation: To cultivate yourself so the people are at ease — even Yao and Shun found that hard.
confucius-14-45b.note: The widest stage is marked with the sages' names to show its limit.

confucius-14-46.translation: Yuan Rang sat waiting with his legs sprawled. The Master said: young and not deferential, grown and with nothing to show, old and not dead — this is a pest. And he tapped his shin with his staff.
confucius-14-46.note: Said to an old friend. The tap of the staff changes the register of the words.

confucius-14-47.translation: A boy of Que village was carrying messages. Someone asked: is he one who seeks to improve? The Master said: I have seen him take a grown man's seat, and seen him walk abreast of his elders. He does not seek improvement; he wants to arrive quickly.
confucius-14-47.note: Two small actions, and he reads what is behind them.
